title.heading: The Great Fire of London
title.lead: What can water do to flames?

picture.shows: The Great Fire of London spreading through seventeenth-century streets
picture.subject: named

slides.heading: Where did it begin?
slides.lead: The Great Fire of London began in a bakery in Pudding Lane in London, in September 1666.

figure.shows: A historical reconstruction of the Pudding Lane bakery where the Great Fire began
figure.subject: named

slides.heading: Wooden houses
slides.lead: Many houses had wooden walls. Wood burns easily, and the houses were close enough for flames to spread.

figure.shows: A historical reconstruction of closely packed timber houses during the Great Fire
figure.subject: named

slides.heading: Strong winds
slides.lead: Strong winds pushed the flames towards other houses. This helped the fire spread through London's streets.

figure.shows: Strong winds driving the Great Fire towards neighbouring timber houses
figure.subject: named

slides.heading: What helped the fire spread through wooden streets?

options.why: The pupil applies the everyday experience of blowing to cool something hot to a large fire.
The pupil treats wooden walls as barriers without recognising that the walls themselves burn.

slides.heading: Water buckets
slides.lead: People carried water in buckets and threw it onto flames. Water could put out small fires.

figure.shows: People using leather water buckets to fight a small fire during the Great Fire of London
figure.subject: named

slides.heading: Pulling houses down
slides.lead: People pulled down houses to make gaps. With less wood to burn, the fire could not spread as easily.

figure.shows: People pulling down a timber house ahead of the Great Fire to create a gap
figure.subject: named

slides.heading: An empty space
slides.lead: Imagine houses beside a fire are removed. Why might this help protect houses beyond?

picture.shows: An imagined row of timber houses with burning houses separated from unburnt houses by a cleared gap
picture.subject: generic

items.question: Write the street and year where the Great Fire began.
Imagine a small fire starts beside a well. How could buckets help?
items.answer: People could fill buckets with water and throw it onto the flames.

slides.heading: Sparks can travel
slides.lead: Strong winds also carried burning sparks through the air. Sparks landing on wood could start another fire.

figure.shows: Wind carrying burning sparks from a burning London house towards another timber roof during the Great Fire
figure.subject: named

items.question: Imagine sparks reach a wooden shed. Why could the shed burn?
items.answer: The sparks could set fire to the wood because wood burns easily.

items.question: Imagine buckets are empty and flames approach. How could removing houses help?
items.answer: Removing houses makes gaps with less wood for the fire to burn.

items.question: Where and when did the Great Fire begin?
Why did removing wooden houses slow the fire?
items.answer: It made gaps with less wood for the fire to burn.
